periods.activity_title: What Does a Letter Stand For? Building the First Expressions

textbook_items_in_class.description: Shabnam is 3 years older than Aftab. Derive the expression s = a + 3 for Shabnam's age from Aftab's; use it to find Shabnam's age when Aftab is 23.
Parthiv's L-shaped matchstick pattern: derive the expression 2n for the number of matchsticks needed to make n L-shapes.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write algebraic expressions for: (a) 5 more than a number; (b) 4 less than a number; (c) 2 less than 13 times a number; (d) 13 less than 2 times a number.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.84
homework.description: Munirathna joins a pipe of unknown length k metres to a 20 m pipe. Write the expression for the combined length.

time_bands.activity: Open with a question: if a friend is always 3 years older than you, how would you write their age without knowing yours? Students share guesses. Introduce the idea that a letter can hold any number — a 'letter-number'. Walk through Example 1, section 4.1 p.81 ("Shabnam is 3 years older than Aftab. Derive the expression s = a + 3…"), reading the table together and naming the expression s = a + 3.

Move to Example 2, section 4.1 p.82 ("Parthiv's L-shaped matchstick pattern: derive the expression 2n…."). Students count matchsticks for 1, 2, 3 L-shapes on rough paper, record in a table, and spot the doubling. Class agrees on 2n as the general formula; establish vocabulary: letter-number, algebraic expression.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.84 ("Write algebraic expressions for: (a) 5 more than a number; (b) 4 less than a number; (c) 2 less than 13 times a number; (d) 13 less than 2 times a number.") individually, then compare with a partner. Discuss how 'less than' reverses the order students expect.

Quick whole-class share: three students read their expressions aloud. Clarify any confusion between 'a less than b' and 'a minus b'. Preview that letter-numbers can also describe costs and shapes — introduce Example 3 briefly as a teaser for the follow-up unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse '4 less than n' with 'n less than 4', writing n – 4 when 4 – n is meant — make the word-order explicit during the Q5 share. Example 3 (Example 3, section 4.1 p.82) extends the idea to two variables and is a useful self-study pointer for students who finish early.
materials: Matchsticks or toothpicks (a small handful per pair)

periods.activity_title: Formulas for Shapes, Costs, and Calendars

textbook_items_in_class.description: Ketaki's coconut-jaggery cost: derive the two-variable expression c × 35 + j × 60 and use it to compute cost for 7 coconuts and 4 kg jaggery.
Perimeter of a square as the formula 4 × q; use it to find the perimeter when sidelength is 7 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write perimeter formulas for: (a) equilateral triangle; (b) regular pentagon; (c) regular hexagon.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the table for total amount Krithika has given counts of ₹100, ₹20, and ₹5 notes, including the general algebraic expression 100x + 20y + 5z.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 4.1 p.85
textbook_items_in_class.description: In a 2 × 3 calendar grid with bottom-middle date 'w', write expressions for the dates in all blank cells.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.84
homework.description: Venkatalakshmi's flour mill: choose the correct expression from (a)–(e) for grinding y kg of grain given 10-second start time and 8-second-per-kg rate.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 4.1 p.85
homework.description: Describe real-world situations corresponding to: (a) 8 × x + 3 × y; (b) 15 × j – 2 × k.

time_bands.activity: Draw a two-column table on the board: 'Situation' and 'Expression'. Walk through Example 3, section 4.1 p.82 ("Ketaki's coconut-jaggery cost: derive the two-variable expression c × 35 + j × 60…"), naming each variable and its meaning before writing the expression. Compute the specific cost together.

Work through Example 4, section 4.1 p.83 ("Perimeter of a square as the formula 4 × q…."). Students extend the pattern with Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.84 ("Write perimeter formulas for: (a) equilateral triangle; (b) regular pentagon; (c) regular hexagon.") — pairs write and verify by drawing shapes.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.84 ("Complete the table for total amount Krithika has given counts of ₹100, ₹20, and ₹5 notes….") in pairs, filling numerical rows first, then writing 100x + 20y + 5z for the general row. Discuss: how is this like the coconut-jaggery formula?

Challenge: Figure it Out Q7, section 4.1 p.85 ("In a 2 × 3 calendar grid with bottom-middle date 'w', write expressions for the dates in all blank cells."). Students draw the grid, mark w, and work out neighbours by adding or subtracting 1 and 7. A few students share their grids; class checks by substituting a real calendar date.

periods.teacher_notes: A common slip when writing multi-variable formulas is omitting one variable entirely — for example, writing 35c for the coconut-jaggery cost and ignoring jaggery. The calendar-grid task sharpens awareness that the same letter-number can anchor many related expressions at once. Figure it Out Q4 (Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.84) makes a strong self-study extension on choosing the correct expression from a list.
materials: Graph paper or blank grids for calendar task

periods.activity_title: Order, Brackets, and the Bridge to Algebra

time_bands.activity: Write 23 – 10 × 2 on the board and ask students silently to compute it. Collect answers — many will write 26 (left-to-right) rather than 3 (multiplication first). Use this disagreement to review why operation order matters, working through the section's first item from Figure it Out, section 4.2 p.85 ("Find the values of the arithmetic expressions: (1) 23 – 10 × 2….").

Model the swap-and-group strategy on item (2) and the bracket-distribute method on item (5) from Figure it Out, section 4.2 p.85 ("…(2) 83 + 28 – 13 + 32; …(5) 68 – (18 + 13)…."), showing both approaches side by side. Emphasise that removing brackets with a negative sign in front flips all inner signs — a rule that will carry directly into algebraic simplification.

Students work independently on items (3), (4), (6), and (7) from Figure it Out, section 4.2 p.85. After each item, a student writes their working on the board and the class checks. If time permits, students attempt item (5) by the distribution route rather than the bracket-first route, comparing both answers.

Close with a brief discussion: what happens if letter-numbers replace the specific digits? Illustrate that 68 – (18 + 13) becomes x – (y + z) and the same negative-sign distribution rule applies. This links arithmetic revision explicitly to the algebraic work.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent error here is left-to-right evaluation ignoring multiplication priority — and a second one is retaining the original sign when distributing a negative bracket (writing – 18 – 13 as – 18 + 13). Watch both in the board-sharing step. The bridge sentence at the close is important: students should leave understanding that arithmetic rules carry unchanged into algebra.

textbook_segments.title: Omission of the Multiplication Symbol in Algebraic Expressions

periods.activity_title: The Silent Times Sign: Reading and Writing 4n

textbook_items_in_class.description: Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: nine algebraic substitutions (e.g. if a = –4, then 10 – a = 6; if d = 6, then 3d = 36; etc.). For each: identify whether there is a mistake, explain what went wrong, and give the correct value.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 4 × n, then 4n. Ask students what changed and why the '×' disappeared. Establish the convention: when a number multiplies a letter-number, the multiplication sign is dropped and the number is written first. Connect to the sequence 4, 8, 12, 16 — students write the nth term as 4n and evaluate for n = 1, 2, 3, 4 to confirm.

Evaluate 7k when k = 4, and 5m + 3 when m = 2, as a class. Stress the substitution procedure: replace the letter with its value inside the expression, then compute. Ask: could you write k7 instead of 7k? Why not? Reinforce that the number precedes the letter always.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 4.3 p.87 ("Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: nine algebraic substitutions….") in pairs. For each of the nine items, pairs must (a) decide if there is a mistake, (b) name what went wrong in a sentence, and (c) write the correct value. Circulate and prompt: Is 3d the same as writing the digit 3 next to the digit 6?

Whole-class share of two or three contested items, especially the concatenation error (3d = 36 when d = 6) and the negative-value error (10 – a = 6 when a = –4). Ask students to articulate the rule in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The concatenation error — reading 3d as 'thirty-d' and writing 36 when d = 6 — is the most damaging misconception in this section; name it explicitly. A second common error is treating 10 – a as 10 – |a| when a is negative, losing the double-negative. Having students write the substitution step 10 – (–4) with explicit parentheses prevents both errors.

textbook_segments.title: Omission of the Multiplication Symbol in Algebraic Expressions

periods.activity_title: From Convention to Simplification: Like Terms at Work

textbook_items_in_class.description: Pencil-eraser shop over three days: simplify 5c + 3c + 10c = 18c using the distributive property; set up 18c + 11d for total earnings.
Big rectangle split into two smaller rectangles: show 4v + 3v = 7v and 12n – 4n = 8n using two methods of computing area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Add the numbers in each of three grid pictures (containing letter-number terms like 5y, x, –6, 2p, 3q, –5g, 5k, etc.). Write corresponding expressions and simplify; try at least two different grouping methods and confirm the same result.

time_bands.activity: Pose a quick scenario: a shop sells pencils at c rupees each — if Mira buys 5 pencils, Renu buys 3, and Anu buys 10, how many pencils were sold in total? Students write 5c + 3c + 10c, then discuss whether this can be written more compactly. Work through Example 5, section 4.4 p.88 ("Pencil-eraser shop over three days: simplify 5c + 3c + 10c = 18c…."), naming the distributive property as the justification.

Draw two rectangles on the board sharing a side — as in Example 6, section 4.4 p.89 ("Big rectangle split into two smaller rectangles: show 4v + 3v = 7v…."). Students compute the area in two ways (add widths first; compute separately and add) and see both routes give 7v. Extend to 12n – 4n = 8n by the same rectangle logic. Establish formally: like terms share the same letter-number, unlike terms do not.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93 ("Add the numbers in each of three grid pictures….") — choosing at least two grouping orders for one grid and confirming identical results. Circulate and ask: which terms can be combined? Which cannot?

Consolidate: students write a one-sentence definition of 'like terms' in their own words. Cold-call two students to share; refine wording as a class so the definition names both the letter and the power (since the chapter will later feature only first-power terms).

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the shorthand convention established for 4n, students now apply distributive thinking to collect like terms — the step from 5c + 3c + 10c = (5 + 3 + 10)c is the key conceptual move. Watch for students who attempt to combine unlike terms such as 5c + 3d into 8cd — the rectangle diagram from Example 6 is the clearest visual counter-argument to offer them.

periods.activity_title: Why Are Two Expressions Equal? Bracket Removal and Proof

textbook_items_in_class.description: Chair-table rental shop: simplify (40x + 75y) – (6x + 10y) to 34x + 65y by distributing the negative sign and collecting like terms.
Show that 5u and 5 + u are not equal by evaluating both for u = 2, 5, 8; similarly compare 10y – 3 and 10(y – 3) for several values of y.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Simplify each expression: (a) p+p+p+p; p+p+p+q; p+q+p–q; (b) p–q+p–q; p+q–p+q; (c) p+q–(p+q); p–q–p–q; (d) 2d–d–d–d; 2d–d–d–c; (e) 2d–d–(d–c); 2d–(d–d)–c; (f) 2d–d–c–c.

Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: eleven algebraic simplifications (e.g. 3a+2b = 5; 6(p+2) = 6p+8; 5–(2–6z) = 3–6z; etc.). For each: identify the mistake, explain it, and give the correct simplest form.

time_bands.activity: State the question clearly: when is (A + B) – (C + D) the same as A + B – C – D, and why? Work through Example 7, section 4.4 p.90 ("Chair-table rental shop: simplify (40x + 75y) – (6x + 10y)…."), annotating each sign change explicitly and asking students to predict each step before writing it.

Pose: are 5u and 5 + u the same expression? Students substitute u = 2, 5, 8 and record both values in a table. Work through Example 10, section 4.4 p.92 ("Show that 5u and 5 + u are not equal…."), establishing that two expressions are equal only when they give identical values for every possible substitution — not just a few. Extend to 10y – 3 versus 10(y – 3).

Students work through selected sub-parts of Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.94 ("Simplify each expression: (a) p+p+p+p; p+p+p+q….") focusing on the bracket-heavy sub-parts (c), (d), (e). For each, students must write the sign-distribution step explicitly before combining like terms.

Introduce Figure it Out, section 4.4 p.94 ("Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: eleven algebraic simplifications….") — read two erroneous items aloud and students write the error name on their slates.

periods.teacher_notes: The core reasoning move here is that the equality of two expressions is a universal claim, not a lucky coincidence for one value — Example 10 drives this home. Watch for students who believe 3a + 2b = 5 because they are thinking of specific values; the 'Mind the Mistake' set in Figure it Out, section 4.4 p.94 is rich with exactly this category of error. Example 8 (Example 8, section 4.4 p.91) is a good self-study pointer for quiz-score addition of multi-term expressions.

periods.activity_title: Simplify, Verify, Correct: Multi-Step Expression Practice

textbook_items_in_class.description: Charu's three-round quiz scores 7p – 3q, 8p – 4q, 6p – 2q: add to get total 21p – 9q; compare with Krishita's 23p – 7q by finding their difference.
Simplify 4(x + y) – y to 4x + 3y using the distributive property.

Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: eleven algebraic simplifications (e.g. 3a+2b = 5; 6(p+2) = 6p+8; 5–(2–6z) = 3–6z; etc.). For each: identify the mistake, explain it, and give the correct simplest form.

homework.description: Sum of all numbers in a symmetric 4×4 grid containing 3, r, s in each quarter: show that three different addition strategies all simplify to 2r + 2s + 24.

time_bands.activity: Work through Example 8, section 4.4 p.91 ("Charu's three-round quiz scores 7p – 3q, 8p – 4q, 6p – 2q: add to get total 21p – 9q….") as a class, adding column by column and then finding the difference with Krishita's total. Establish the procedure: align like terms, add coefficients, handle subtraction of the whole expression.

Work through Example 9, section 4.4 p.92 ("Simplify 4(x + y) – y to 4x + 3y…."), asking students to expand the bracket before combining. Pose: what if the expression were 4(x + y) + y? Students predict and check.

Students work through all eleven items in Figure it Out, section 4.4 p.94 ("Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: eleven algebraic simplifications….") individually. For each item they write: (a) error type in a few words, (b) the corrected expression. Pairs swap and check each other's corrections.

Class debrief: which error appeared most often? Vote by show of hands across: sign-flip error, unlike-term combination, and bracket-expansion error. The majority error is named as 'the one to watch' going forward.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who can simplify straightforward like-term sums often stumble when the bracket carries a negative sign into multiple unlike terms — 6(p + 2) = 6p + 8 instead of 6p + 12 is a classic example in this exercise set. The peer-swap check in pairs surfaces errors that self-checking often misses. Example 11 (Example 11, section 4.4 p.93) is assigned as a self-study pointer: the symmetric grid is a beautiful multi-strategy application of everything in this section.

periods.activity_title: Detective Work: Formulas Behind Patterns and Grids

textbook_items_in_class.description: Saree-border repeating pattern A, B, C, D, E, F: derive that design C appears at position 3n, design B at 3n – 1, design A at 3n – 2; use remainder on division by 3 to identify designs at positions 99, 122, 148.

Formula Detective: find the formulas for two number machines shown (input-output diagrams with 4–5 pairs each) and write the algebraic expression for each set of inputs, including the general a, b expression.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 4.5 p.104
textbook_items_in_class.description: Traffic signal colour sequence (R, G, Y, R, G, Y, …): find the colour at positions 90, 190, and 343; write expressions for positions of each colour.

time_bands.activity: Draw a repeating pattern on the board: a sequence of shapes or colours cycling in groups of 3. Ask: can we predict the 99th member without listing all 99? Work through Example 12, section 4.5 p.96 ("Saree-border repeating pattern A, B, C, D, E, F: derive that design C appears at position 3n…."), building the position formulas from the period-3 cycle structure using the remainder idea.

Students tackle Figure it Out, section 4.5 p.95 ("Formula Detective: find the formulas for two number machines….") in pairs — studying input-output pairs, guessing the rule, testing on a new input, then writing the algebraic expression. Pairs share their formulas and the class tests each formula on the provided pairs.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q13, section 4.5 p.104 ("Traffic signal colour sequence (R, G, Y, R, G, Y, …): find the colour at positions 90, 190, and 343…."). They write position expressions for each colour using the remainder method from Example 12. Compare: how is this exactly like the saree-border reasoning?

Bring together: in both the saree pattern and the traffic signal, the algebraic expression does the work of checking infinitely many cases at once. Students write one sentence stating why an algebraic proof is more powerful than just listing examples.

periods.teacher_notes: The insight that remainder on division by the cycle length identifies the position within the cycle is the key reasoning move — students who miss it revert to listing, which fails for large positions like 148 or 343. Watch for students who write 3n for all positions in a 3-cycle rather than distinguishing 3n, 3n – 1, and 3n – 2. The calendar 2 × 2 diagonal proof (discussed in the prose of section 4.5) is an elegant complementary example for students who wish to explore further.
materials: Coloured markers for pattern demonstration on board

periods.activity_title: Four Problems, One Chapter: Expressions at Work
periods.teacher_notes: Refer to Prepared Table (see material: 'Problems and solutions') for the problems in full and their worked solutions. Pose all four problems on the board at once. Students work individually with full written working, then compare with a neighbour — any disagreement is reconstructed step by step, not just checked answer-to-answer. Four students present (one per problem); after each presentation the class names the chapter method the solution used. Problem 1 needs expression-writing from a real situation (section 4.1). Problem 2 needs substitution and sign-awareness when evaluating an expression (section 4.3). Problem 3 needs like-term collection and bracket removal (section 4.4). Problem 4 needs deriving a general formula from a growing pattern and inverting it to identify a specific term (section 4.5). Watch for: in Problem 2, students who compute 10 − 3(−3) as 10 − 9 = 1 instead of 10 + 9 = 19; in Problem 3, students who distribute −3 as +3 into the bracket; in Problem 4, students who count all sides of every hexagon rather than the new sides each additional hexagon contributes.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | A school tuck shop sells samosas at ₹8 each and juice boxes at ₹15 each. Write an expression for the total amount earned when s samosas and j juice boxes are sold. Use it to find the total when 12 samosas and 7 juice boxes are sold. | Expression: 8s + 15j. Substitute s = 12, j = 7: 8 × 12 + 15 × 7 = 96 + 105 = ₹201.
2 | Evaluate the expression 10 − 3k for k = −3, k = 0, and k = 4. Which value of k makes the expression equal to 22? | k = −3: 10 − 3(−3) = 10 + 9 = 19. k = 0: 10 − 0 = 10. k = 4: 10 − 12 = −2. For 10 − 3k = 22: 3k = −12, so k = −4. Check: 10 − 3(−4) = 10 + 12 = 22. ✓
3 | Simplify: (5a + 8b − 3) + (2a − 4b + 7) − 3(a − 2b). | Expand the bracket: −3(a − 2b) = −3a + 6b. Collect like terms: a-terms: 5a + 2a − 3a = 4a. b-terms: 8b − 4b + 6b = 10b. Constants: −3 + 7 = 4. Result: 4a + 10b + 4.
4 | Hexagons are placed in a row, sharing one side with the next. The first hexagon needs 6 matchsticks; each new one adds 5. How many matchsticks are needed for n hexagons? How many for 20 hexagons? A position in the sequence has 96 matchsticks — which hexagon number is that? | Each hexagon after the first shares one side, so adds 5 sticks. For 1 hexagon: 6. For n hexagons: 6 + 5(n − 1) = 5n + 1. For n = 20: 5(20) + 1 = 101. For 96 matchsticks: 5n + 1 = 96 → 5n = 95 → n = 19. The 19th hexagon.

materials: Board and chalk or whiteboard markers

time_bands.activity: Write all four problems on the board. Read each aloud clearly. Tell the class: work every problem yourself first, showing every step — answers without working will not be shared in the group comparison.

Individual silent work. Students attempt all four problems with full written working. Move through the room without giving answers; if a student is stuck, ask them to re-read the problem and identify what quantity the letter stands for.

Pair comparison. Each student reads their neighbour's working for the problem they found hardest. Where answers differ, both students reconstruct the solution from the first line — neither simply copies the other's answer. Pairs flag any step they cannot agree on.

Four presentations, one per problem. Each presenter writes their solution on the board and reads it aloud. After each, the class names the chapter method the solution used (expression-writing from a situation; substitution and evaluation; like-term collection and bracket removal; pattern formula and general term). Any unresolved disagreement from the pair stage is cleared here, with the class deciding which step is correct and why.
Close with a single sentence: a letter-number stands for any value, so one expression does the work of infinitely many calculations — that is why every problem today yielded to the same idea.

items.prompt: Which algebraic expression correctly represents '7 less than 4 times a number n'?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify '4 times n' as 4n, then subtract 7 to get 4n – 7.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student reversed the subtraction order, writing 7 – 4n instead of 4n – 7, misreading 'less than' as 'minus from the left'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student did not apply the multiplication correctly, treating '4 times n' as simply adding 4 and n before subtracting 7.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student grouped the subtraction inside a bracket with 4 as a factor, confusing '4 times a number, then subtract 7' with '4 times (number minus 7)'.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the phrase word by word and match each word to a symbol before writing the expression.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a real-world sentence whose cost or distance situation would be described by 4n – 7.

exercise.description: Write algebraic expressions for: (a) 5 more than a number; (b) 4 less than a number; (c) 2 less than 13 times a number; (d) 13 less than 2 times a number.

items.section_title: Omission of the Multiplication Symbol in Algebraic Expressions
items.prompt: A student writes: 'If m = 5, then 6m = 65.' Which statement correctly identifies what went wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: The student applied the wrong operation: 6m means 6 ÷ m, so the answer should be 1.2.

options.label: B
options.text: The student confused the shorthand 6m with writing the digit 6 next to the digit 5, treating multiplication as concatenation; the correct value is 6 × 5 = 30.

options.label: C
options.text: The student forgot to add 6 and 5, so the answer should be 11.

options.label: D
options.text: There is no mistake; 6m = 65 is correct when m = 5.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student confused concatenation with multiplication. 6m means 6 × m, so when m = 5 the correct value is 6 × 5 = 30, not 65.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the convention that 6m means 6 × m and substitute: 6 × 5 = 30.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks the shorthand means addition rather than multiplication, a fundamental misreading of algebraic notation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student incorrectly interprets the position of the numeral as indicating division rather than multiplication.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not recognised any error, suggesting they share the same concatenation misconception as the fictional student in the prompt.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to look back at the worked examples in section 4.3 and verify what 6m means by evaluating 6 × 1, 6 × 2, 6 × 3.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to create two more 'Mind the Mistake' items of their own involving this type of error, with correct answers provided.

exercise.description: Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: nine algebraic substitutions (e.g. if a = –4, then 10 – a = 6; if d = 6, then 3d = 36; etc.). For each: identify whether there is a mistake, explain what went wrong, and give the correct value.

items.prompt: A student claims that 5a + 3b simplifies to 8ab. Explain why this claim is wrong and state what the fully simplified form actually is.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5a and 3b are unlike terms because they contain different letter-numbers. Unlike terms cannot be combined by adding their coefficients. The expression 5a + 3b is already in its simplest form and cannot be written as a single term.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check that terms share the same letter-number before combining; since a and b differ, 5a + 3b cannot be simplified further.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to talk through the rectangle-area argument from Example 6 — areas of rectangles with different side lengths cannot be merged into one rectangle.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if you alter one term so that the expression does simplify to a single term, what is the minimum change needed, and what does the new expression mean?

exercise.description: Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake: eleven algebraic simplifications (e.g. 3a+2b = 5; 6(p+2) = 6p+8; 5–(2–6z) = 3–6z; etc.). For each: identify the mistake, explain it, and give the correct simplest form.

items.prompt: A sequence of shapes follows a repeating cycle of 4: Star, Circle, Triangle, Square, Star, Circle, Triangle, Square, … . A student says: 'The 50th shape must be a Star because 50 ÷ 4 = 12 remainder 2, and Stars are in position 1.' Explain clearly whether the student's reasoning is correct or incorrect, and determine what the 50th shape actually is. Justify your answer using an algebraic expression for the position of each shape in the cycle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student's arithmetic is correct (50 ÷ 4 = 12 remainder 2) but the interpretation is wrong. A remainder of 2 means the 50th position falls on the 2nd element of the cycle, which is Circle, not Star. Stars occupy positions where the remainder on division by 4 is 1 (positions 4n – 3 for whole-number n). Circles occupy positions where the remainder is 2 (positions 4n – 2). Therefore the 50th shape is a Circle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the position by the cycle length, interpret the remainder as the within-cycle position, and match to the corresponding element.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student list the first 8 positions with their shapes in a table, then identify which remainder each shape always produces.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what is the algebraic expression for positions of Triangles? Use it to find the largest Triangle-position below 200.

exercise.description: Formula Detective: find the formulas for two number machines shown (input-output diagrams with 4–5 pairs each) and write the algebraic expression for each set of inputs, including the general a, b expression.

items.prompt: A garden has rows of rose plants. Each row has p plants. There are also 5 sunflower plants along the fence. Write an algebraic expression for the total number of plants when there are r rows of roses. Then find the total when r = 6 and p = 8.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total plants = r × p + 5. When r = 6 and p = 8: total = 6 × 8 + 5 = 48 + 5 = 53 plants.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Form the expression by multiplying number of rows by plants per row and adding the fixed sunflower count, then substitute the given values.

inclusivity.support: Suggest drawing a diagram with 2 rows of 3 circles each plus 5 squares along the side to build the expression from a picture before substituting.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the constraint: the fence now has g sunflower plants and each row has q roses. Write the expression for 10 rows and evaluate for g = 7, q = 9.

items.prompt: Evaluate the expression 56 – (14 + 9) + 3 × 5, showing each step of your working clearly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1 — bracket: 14 + 9 = 23. Step 2 — multiplication: 3 × 5 = 15. Step 3 — left to right: 56 – 23 + 15 = 33 + 15 = 48.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply operation-order rules: evaluate the bracket first, then the multiplication, then add and subtract left to right.

inclusivity.support: Provide a number line or stepped written frame: bracket result → multiplication result → final addition/subtraction.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one number so the final answer is exactly 50. Which number did you change, and by how much?

items.section_title: Omission of the Multiplication Symbol in Algebraic Expressions
items.prompt: Evaluate the expression 9k – 4 when k = 3, and evaluate 3h + 7 when h = 5. Then find the sum of the two results.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Replace each letter-number with its given value using the multiplication shorthand convention, then compute each expression and add the results.

inclusivity.support: Write the substitution step explicitly with the multiplication sign reinstated (9 × 3 – 4) before computing, to avoid the concatenation error.
inclusivity.challenge: Find values of k and h (both positive whole numbers) such that 9k – 4 equals 3h + 7. Is there more than one pair? Explain.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93
exercise.description: Add the numbers in each of three grid pictures (containing letter-number terms like 5y, x, –6, 2p, 3q, –5g, 5k, etc.). Write corresponding expressions and simplify; try at least two different grouping methods and confirm the same result.

items.prompt: Simplify the expression (7p + 4q) – (3p – 2q) + 5q, showing each step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1 — distribute the negative: (7p + 4q) – 3p + 2q + 5q. Step 2 — collect p-terms: 7p – 3p = 4p. Step 3 — collect q-terms: 4q + 2q + 5q = 11q. Simplified result: 4p + 11q.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Distribute the negative sign across the second bracket, then collect like terms separately for p and q.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to underline p-terms in one colour and q-terms in another before combining, to avoid mixing unlike terms.
inclusivity.challenge: Subtract one further expression of your own choice so that the q-terms cancel out completely; what did you subtract?

items.prompt: A snail climbs 8 cm up a wall each day and slips back 3 cm each night. Write an algebraic expression for the snail's net distance from the start after exactly 7 days and 7 nights. Calculate its value. What would happen to the net distance if the slip distance were greater than the climb distance?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each day-night cycle the snail gains 8 – 3 = 5 cm. After 7 full cycles (7 days and 7 nights) the net distance = 7 × (8 – 3) = 7 × 5 = 35 cm. Algebraic expression with climb u and slip d: net distance = 7(u – d). If d > u then u – d is negative, meaning the net distance becomes negative — the snail moves further from its start, i.e. it ends up below its starting point.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Form the net-gain-per-cycle expression (climb – slip), multiply by the number of cycles, and substitute the given values.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line showing one day's climb and one night's slip to visualise the net gain per cycle before writing the expression.
inclusivity.challenge: Write a general expression for the net distance after n day-night cycles with climb u and slip d, and determine for which values of n the snail first exceeds 100 cm when u = 8 and d = 3.
